blocks.content: Think of the internet as a massive postal system carrying billions of messages at once. For any message to reach the right destination, every device needs its own distinct address, without that, there would be no way to tell one recipient from another among billions.

An IP address is exactly that, a unique number assigned to every device on a network, acting like a digital home address. This topic covers how IP addresses actually work, the difference between IPv4 and IPv6, subnetting and CIDR, public versus private addressing and NAT, and how routers actually decide where a packet goes next.
1. What an IP Address Actually Is
blocks.text: 1. What an IP Address Actually Is

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273060736-272460879.png
blocks.alt: An IP address is a packet's end to end identity for the whole journey, a MAC address only matters for the current local hop

blocks.content: Every packet crossing the internet carries two pieces of information on its envelope, where it came from and where it is going. Those are IP addresses, numerical labels identifying every device connected to a network. Routers use the destination IP address to forward a packet hop by hop across the internet until it finally arrives.

blocks.title: Two Different Jobs
blocks.content: The IP address is the packet's end to end identity, it never changes for the entire journey. The MAC address only ever matters for the current local hop, and it changes at every single router along the way, since each router replaces the source and destination MAC addresses before handing the packet to the next link.
2. IPv4: The 32 Bit Address
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273063121-609011956.png
blocks.alt: An IPv4 address is four eight bit numbers, each ranging from 0 to 255, separated by dots

blocks.content: IPv4 has been the foundation of the internet since the early 1980s. An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, written as four decimal numbers separated by dots, each one representing eight bits, an octet, ranging from 0 to 255.

4.3 billion addresses seemed enormous in 1981. Today there are over 15 billion connected devices, phones, laptops, smart TVs, cars, sensors. IPv4 ran out long ago, and the internet survives through subnetting, private addresses, and NAT.
3. Subnetting and CIDR
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273064994-786713611.png
blocks.alt: An IP address splits into a network portion, identifying which network, and a host portion, identifying which device on it

blocks.content: An IP address has two parts, a network portion, which network, and a host portion, which device on that network. The subnet mask defines exactly where that split happens.

CIDR, Classless Inter-Domain Routing, notation writes that split as a number after a slash. 10.0.0.0/24 means the first 24 bits identify the network, and the remaining 8 bits identify individual hosts, giving 256 total addresses on that network.

blocks.title: A Real Cloud Network Layout
blocks.text: A larger network like 10.0.0.0/16 is created first, giving 65,536 IP addresses. That large block is then divided into smaller subnets based on need, one subnet for web servers, one for application servers, one for databases, and a smaller one for a bastion host. Each subnet gets its own isolated range, which helps organize resources, improve security, and manage scale cleanly. A /20 network like 10.10.0.0/20 gives 4096 addresses total, 4094 of them usable once the network and broadcast addresses are excluded.

blocks.content: Why CIDR matters in high level design: when you design a private network, you choose a CIDR block upfront. Too small and you run out of addresses as you scale. Too large and you cannot cleanly connect it to another network whose range overlaps yours.
4. Public vs Private IP Addresses
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024509-74661948.png
blocks.alt: A private IP address only exists inside a local network, reaching the public internet only through the router's own public IP

blocks.content: Not all IP addresses are equal. Some can be reached from anywhere on the internet, others only exist within a private network and stay invisible to the outside world entirely.

A public IP is globally unique, assigned by an internet authority, and only one device in the world can hold that exact address at a time. These are reachable from anywhere, which is why public facing servers use them, though public addresses themselves are limited and scarce.

Private IPs are reserved ranges used only inside local networks, including 10.x.x.x, 172.16.x.x through 172.31.x.x, and 192.168.x.x. They are never routed over the public internet, and because they stay local, the exact same private address, like 192.168.1.10, can exist in millions of different homes without ever conflicting.
NAT: How Private Devices Reach the Internet
blocks.text: NAT: How Private Devices Reach the Internet

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273068746-3392831.png
blocks.alt: Network Address Translation rewrites a private device's source IP to the router's own public IP before it leaves the local network

blocks.content: If a private IP can never leave your network, how does a phone on a private address still reach the public internet? Through Network Address Translation. Your router holds one public IP from your internet provider, and every outgoing request from a private device has its source IP rewritten to that public address. The router tracks which internal device made each request and routes the reply back to exactly the right one.

blocks.title: NAT Kept IPv4 Alive
blocks.content: NAT is what kept the internet running long after IPv4 addresses should have run out entirely, letting billions of devices share a far smaller pool of public addresses. The trade off is that NAT breaks true end to end connectivity and complicates certain protocols that expect a stable, reachable address.
5. IPv6: The Permanent Fix
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024508-735122916.png
blocks.alt: A modern device prefers IPv6, globally unique and NAT free, and falls back to IPv4 through NAT only when IPv6 is unavailable

blocks.content: IPv6 uses 128 bit addresses, four times larger than IPv4, written as eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons, for example 2404:6800:4007:80e::200e. The total address space is roughly 340 undecillion addresses, comfortably more than every grain of sand on every beach on earth.

Because IPv4 addresses are scarce, it depends on NAT to share them. IPv6 instead gives every device its own unique global address, so NAT is not needed at all. Most networks today run dual stack, supporting both and preferring IPv6 whenever it is available.
6. Special Addresses You Will See Constantly
blocks.text: 6. Special Addresses You Will See Constantly

blocks.content: {"headers":["Address","Meaning"],"rows":[["127.0.0.1, loopback","Routes traffic back to your own machine, used for localhost and local testing, never leaves the system"],["0.0.0.0, unspecified","Means all interfaces on a machine, a server listening on 0.0.0.0:8080 listens on every IP it has"],["169.254.x.x, link local","Auto assigned when DHCP fails, meaning the device could not get an address from the network"],["255.255.255.255, broadcast","Sends a message to every device on the local network, used during DHCP discovery"],["10.x, 172.16 to 31.x, 192.168.x, private","Used only inside private networks, common in home WiFi, cloud networks, and containers"]]}

A useful debugging shortcut: seeing 169.254.x.x on a device means DHCP is broken or the network is unreachable. Seeing 127.0.0.1 in a connection error usually means the app is misconfigured to talk to itself instead of the intended remote service.
7. How IP Routing Actually Works
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273072839-878923547.png
blocks.alt: A packet does not know its full path upfront, each router makes an independent forwarding decision until the destination is reached

blocks.content: A packet does not know its full path ahead of time. Each router makes an entirely independent decision, read the destination IP, check its own routing table, send it to the next best hop, and the packet bounces forward, router to router, until it arrives.
Longest Prefix Match
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025329-471781764.png
blocks.alt: When several routes match the same destination, the router always picks the most specific one, the longest prefix

blocks.content: When multiple routing table entries all match a destination, a router always picks the most specific one, the longest prefix. Given a destination like 10.10.5.44, matching routes for 10.0.0.0/8, 10.10.0.0/16, and 10.10.5.0/24 all apply at once, and the /24 route wins, since a larger prefix number, /24 over /16 over /8, means a more specific, more precise match. If nothing matches at all, the router falls back to its default route, conventionally written 0.0.0.0/0.

The example below implements exactly this decision: given a small routing table and a destination address, it picks the single most specific matching route, falling back to a default route when nothing else matches.
TTL: Packets Do Not Live Forever
blocks.text: TTL: Packets Do Not Live Forever

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273076306-16466535.png
blocks.alt: Traceroute works by deliberately sending packets with a rising TTL, forcing each router along the path to reply in turn

blocks.content: Every IP packet carries a Time To Live counter. Each router decrements it by one, and when it hits zero, the packet is dropped and the router sends back a time exceeded message. This single mechanism prevents a routing loop from circulating a packet forever, and it is also exactly how the traceroute tool reveals a path: sending a packet with TTL 1 gets a reply from the first router, TTL 2 from the second, and so on, continuing until the real destination finally responds.
BGP: How the Internet Stays Connected
blocks.text: BGP: How the Internet Stays Connected

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024986-623452182.png
blocks.alt: A mistakenly withdrawn set of routes can make an entire network vanish from the rest of the internet within minutes

blocks.content: The internet is thousands of independently run networks, called Autonomous Systems, each with its own identity. BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is how these networks tell each other which addresses they can reach and through which path.

blocks.title: A Real BGP Outage
blocks.content: In October 2021, engineers at a major platform accidentally withdrew all of their BGP route announcements during routine maintenance. Every router on the internet deleted that network from its own routing table within minutes. Nobody anywhere could reach it, not because any server crashed, but because the rest of the internet was told, correctly, that the path there no longer existed.

BGP is simultaneously the most critical and the most fragile protocol the internet depends on. A single misconfigured route announcement can make an entire network disappear, which is why real BGP changes are made with extreme care.
Key Takeaway

An IP address is a device's end to end identity across the entire journey of a packet, distinct from the MAC address that only matters for the current local hop. IPv4's 32 bits ran out long ago and survive today through subnetting, private addressing, and NAT, while IPv6's 128 bits give every device a genuinely unique global address with no NAT required at all. Routing itself comes down to one repeated decision at every hop, the most specific matching route wins, and the handful of special addresses, loopback, unspecified, link local, and broadcast, are worth recognizing on sight the moment something looks wrong.
